note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in AK.json, gathered 2026-10-05. "review" holds research notes for a human check; "issues" lists open questions.

byways.name: Alaska Marine Highway: Inside Passage Routes
byways.designation: All-American Road and Alaska Scenic Byway
byways.where: Alaska Marine Highway ferry routes through Southeast Alaska from the British Columbia line north to Skagway and Haines

facts.fact: All routes of the Alaska Marine Highway System are, taken together, an All-American Road.
The Inside Passage runs from the Queen Charlotte Islands of British Columbia north to Skagway, and more than 1,500 islands shelter it from Pacific swells.
Petersburg is known as Alaska's Little Norway, and Wrangell's Petroglyph Beach State Historic Park has the densest group of petroglyphs in Southeast Alaska.
The All-American Road covers more than 3,500 miles of ferry routes serving 35 communities.

byways.review: The catalog has one entry for the whole Alaska Marine Highway; both state program members (Inside Passage and Southcentral/Southwest) map to it. Marine route, not in the DOT&PF road layer.

byways.name: Alaska Railroad
byways.where: Alaska Railroad main line Seward to Fairbanks via Anchorage, Talkeetna, Denali and Nenana, with the Whittier spur

facts.fact: Completed in 1923, the main line runs about 470 miles from tidewater at Seward north to Fairbanks.
It is one of the last flag-stop passenger lines in the United States, stopping wherever passengers want to get on or off.
President Warren G. Harding drove the golden spike at Nenana in 1923, and the line crosses Hurricane Gulch near Milepost 284.

byways.review: A rail line, not a road; not in the DOT&PF road layer.

byways.name: Copper River Highway
byways.where: AK 10 east from the Cordova ferry terminal along the Copper River Delta toward the Million Dollar Bridge and Childs Glacier, about 50 mi

facts.fact: From 1911 to 1938 the Copper River and Northwestern Railway hauled copper ore to Cordova; the highway now uses the lower 52 miles of the abandoned railbed.
The Copper River Delta covers 584 square miles and is a home or stopover for more than 500,000 migratory birds.
The failed bridge at Mile 36 is not passable, and the highway beyond it has been effectively abandoned since 2011.

byways.review: Closed to vehicles at the Mile 36 bridge; DOT&PF page says a replacement is at least three years away and boat shuttles were being permitted.

byways.name: Dalton Highway
byways.where: AK 11, 414 mi from the Elliott Highway north of Fairbanks via the Yukon River, Coldfoot and Atigun Pass to Deadhorse

facts.fact: It is the only road in the United States to cross the Yukon River, the Arctic Circle and the Brooks Range, and it began as a haul road for the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.
Atigun Pass in the Brooks Range is the highest highway pass in Alaska at 4,800 feet; the road is mostly gravel with steep grades.
The Dalton runs 414 miles from the Elliott Highway north of Fairbanks to Deadhorse near Prudhoe Bay.

byways.name: Glenn Highway
byways.designation: National Scenic Byway and Alaska Scenic Byway
byways.where: AK 1 from Anchorage via Palmer and the Matanuska River valley to Eureka Summit, about 135 mi

facts.fact: The byway runs 135 miles and follows the braided Matanuska River for more than half its length.
Palmer's colony farms date from the 1935 New Deal farming experiment.
At Eureka Summit, the end of the byway, four ranges are in view: the Alaska Range and the Chugach, Talkeetna and Wrangell-St. Elias mountains.

byways.name: Haines Highway
byways.designation: National Scenic Byway and Alaska Scenic Byway
byways.where: AK 7 from Haines (and Lutak Road from the ferry terminal) up the Chilkat River to the Canadian border, about 44 mi

facts.fact: First used by the Chilkat Indians, the route became a packhorse trail to the Klondike goldfields in the late 1880s and a U.S. Army access road in 1943.
Hundreds of eagles roost in the cottonwoods along the highway between October and January, and fish wheels work the Chilkat River in June.
From October to February more than 3,500 bald eagles gather in the 48,000-acre Alaska Chilkat Bald Eagle Preserve to feed on late-spawning salmon.

byways.name: Kachemak Bay Route
byways.where: By water across Kachemak Bay from the Homer Spit to Seldovia

facts.fact: The route crosses Kachemak Bay to Seldovia, passing Gull Island with its thousands of nesting birds.
Augustine Island, Mt. Iliamna and Mt. Redoubt rise to the west across about seventy miles of open water, and all three have erupted within the last two decades.
Seldovia sits with its bay in front and the Seldovia Slough behind; sea otters and sea lions frequent the near-shore waters.

byways.review: Marine route; no line in the DOT&PF road layer and no catalog entry. Not drawn.

byways.name: Parks Highway
byways.designation: National Scenic Byway and Alaska Scenic Byway
byways.where: AK 3; DOT&PF layer maps the byway from the Denali State Park boundary (MP 132) to the Healy spur road, about 115 mi; FHWA describes 230 mi Anchorage to Fairbanks

facts.fact: Completed in 1971 as the Anchorage-Fairbanks Highway, it was renamed for George A. Parks, territorial governor of Alaska from 1925 to 1933.
Highlights include Byers Lake and the Alaska Veterans Memorial in Denali State Park, the Hurricane Gulch Bridge, and Broad Pass at 2,400 feet.
The highway gives access to Denali National Park and Preserve, and Healy has Alaska's largest coal-mining operation.

byways.review: Extent disagrees: DOT&PF GIS layer has the byway only from the Denali State Park boundary to Healy (about 115 mi); FHWA lists 230 mi; catalog line is 226 mi.

byways.name: Prince of Wales Island Road System
byways.where: Craig/Klawock/Hollis Highway, Hydaburg Highway, Big Salt Lake, Thorne Bay, Kasaan, North Prince of Wales (USFS 20), Sandy Beach, Coffman Cove, 12 Mile Arm and Port Saint Nicholas roads, Prince of Wales Island

facts.fact: The island is reached by the Inter-Island Ferry Authority and has the most extensive road system in the Tongass National Forest.
About 200 miles of paved road girdle the island; there are totem pole parks in Klawock, Hydaburg and Kasaan, and El Capitan Caves in karst country at the north end.
Four federally recognized tribal governments are on the island: Craig Community Association, Hydaburg Cooperative Association, Organized Village of Kasaan and Klawock Cooperative Association.

byways.review: DOT&PF layer records the road system as 11 named roads designated 2010-05-28, totalling about 211 mi; the DOT&PF page says 260 mi; catalog line is 236 mi.

byways.name: Richardson Highway: north segment
byways.where: AK 2 from Big Delta Road near Fort Greely and Delta Junction north to Fairbanks, about 99 mi

facts.fact: The Richardson is Alaska's oldest highway: a gold rush trail to Eagle in 1898, upgraded to a wagon road in 1910 under General Wilds P. Richardson, and paved in 1957.
Big Delta State Historical Park preserves the restored Rika's Roadhouse, a military telegraph station and early highway work camps.
Santa Claus House in North Pole has a 42-foot Santa Claus dating to the early 1960s.

byways.review: The catalog's Richardson Highway line covers the whole road, Valdez to Fairbanks (364 mi), including about 150 undesignated miles between Glennallen and Delta Junction. DOT&PF layer value for this segment: Byway_Name = 'RICHARDSON HIGHWAY-NORTH SEGMENT' (designated 2004-12-23).

byways.name: Seward Highway
byways.designation: All-American Road, National Forest Scenic Byway and Alaska Scenic Byway
byways.where: 127 mi from Anchorage along Turnagain Arm and over the Kenai Peninsula to Seward

facts.fact: The 127-mile highway holds three designations: USDA Forest Service Scenic Byway, Alaska Scenic Byway and All-American Road.
The first 50 miles skirt the Chugach Mountains and Turnagain Arm, where beluga whales, Dall sheep and bore tides are often seen.
Spruce trees along the arm died when the ground dropped in the 1964 earthquake and left them standing in salt water.

byways.name: Steese Highway
byways.where: AK 6 from the Elliott Highway at Fox via Central to Circle on the Yukon River, about 145 mi

facts.fact: Gold Dredge Number 8, a five-deck, 250-foot dredge, is a National Historic Site along the route.
Circle was the largest settlement on the Yukon before the Klondike rush; miners thought it sat on the Arctic Circle, but it is about 50 miles south.
The highway, completed in 1927, is paved for about the first 81 miles and turns to dirt and gravel around Central.

byways.name: Sterling Highway: north segment
byways.where: AK 1 from the Seward Highway at Tern Lake via Cooper Landing to Skilak Lake Road, about 38 mi

facts.fact: The route runs beside blue-green Kenai Lake to Cooper Landing, with sportfishing on the Kenai and Russian rivers.
Skilak Lake Road is an 18-mile alternate through the Skilak Lake Special Management Area.
The Sterling Highway leaves the Seward Highway at Tern Lake Junction, 90 miles south of Anchorage.

byways.review: The catalog's Sterling Highway line (66 mi) matches the two designated segments together; both members map to it.

byways.name: Taylor & Top of the World Highways
byways.where: AK 5: Taylor Highway from Tetlin Junction to Jack Wade Junction (about 93 mi), then Top of the World Highway to the Canadian border at Boundary (about 13 mi)

facts.fact: The road crosses the Fortymile gold district, and Chicken was named by settlers unable to spell ptarmigan.
Both highways are mostly gravel with steep, narrow grades, and there is no winter maintenance.
The Taylor Highway leaves the Alaska Highway at Tetlin Junction, about 11 miles east of Tok.

byways.review: The Taylor north of Jack Wade Junction to Eagle is not part of the byway.

byways.name: Walden Point Road
byways.where: 14.7 mi from Annette Bay to Metlakatla, Annette Island Reserve

facts.fact: The road runs 14.7 miles from Annette Bay to Metlakatla past many waterfalls, with Sitka black-tailed deer common on the muskeg side.
Annette Island Reserve began in 1887 when Tsimshian people came from British Columbia with missionary William Duncan; recognized in 1891, it is the only Indian reserve in Alaska.
Work began in 1998 and the Department of Defense finished the road early in 2010 as an innovative readiness training project.

byways.review: DOT&PF page URL is byways-metlakatla.shtml and titles it 'Metlakatla: Walden Point Road'.

issues: Catalog richardson-highway-12397 draws the whole Richardson Highway Valdez-Fairbanks (364 mi); only the south segment (Valdez-Glennallen, 118 mi, 1998) and north segment (Delta Junction/Fort Greely-Fairbanks, about 99 mi, 2004) are designated. The roughly 150 mi between Glennallen and Delta Junction is not. Consider redrawing from the DOT&PF layer.
Parks Highway extent disagrees: DOT&PF layer has only Denali State Park boundary (MP 132) to Healy (about 115 mi); FHWA's page describes a 230-mi byway Anchorage-Fairbanks; catalog line is 226 mi.
Copper River Highway is impassable at the failed Mile 36 bridge (closed since 2011 per Wikipedia); DOT&PF page carries an undated note saying the replacement is at least three years away.
Kachemak Bay Route (Homer-Seldovia by water) has no catalog entry and no line in any agency layer; designation date and operator are not given on the DOT&PF page.
Prince of Wales mileage disagrees: DOT&PF text 260 mi, DOT&PF layer about 211 mi, catalog 236 mi.
The program page still links byways-sterling.shtml, which returns 404; the live pages are byways-sterling-north.shtml and byways-sterling-south.shtml.
Haines eagle counts differ: DOT&PF page says 3,000, FHWA says more than 3,500; blurb uses FHWA.

Denali Highway is in the catalog as a Classic drive and is not a state byway; skipped. No catalog road in Alaska sits outside the state program, so there is no second program (Seward Highway's National Forest Scenic Byway status is covered in its member entry).
Many outbound links on the DOT&PF byway pages are http only or old (e.g. fs.fed.us/r10/chugach).
